newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Aussie dlr drifts, samurai wave meets US$ tide.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Aussie dlr drifts, samurai wave meets US$ tide.

text.p: The Australian dollar drifted to a steady finish Tuesday as market flows eddied in the wake of US$/yen volatility and a steady stream of samurai issues.
The currency was suffering in sympathy with its U.S. counterpart as investors continued to trim short yen positions in response to the apparent wishes of the G2, traders said.

But it was not without support in the form of local exporter bids and demand linked to the issue of yet more yen/A$ samurai bonds which were still popular with Japanese investors despite a narrowing in the yield gap. The net result was deadlock and confinement to a US$0.7850/7910 trading range for a while yet.

By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the dollar had dropped anchor at US$0.7879/84 having been becalmed in a US$0.7866/81 range all day. It did make it as high as US$0.7905 offshore Monday after finishing here at US$0.7875/80, but could not sustain the rally in the face of a weakening US$/yen.
The U.S. currency was down at 111.21/26 yen after sliding from 111.95/00 late Monday and levels atop 114.00 last week.
The local unit, as part of an informal dollar bloc, followed at first to reach a 87.21 low from Monday's 87.95/05, but bounced to 87.68/78 on the back of samurai demand both actual and expected.

Traders said a small 10-15 billion yen dual currency samurai issue went through in the morning and it looked like a sizeable 50 billion yen bond was being priced for Ontario Hydro in the afternoon. There was also talk a 30 billion yen issue was coming soon on behalf of the province of Alberta.
The flow of new issues suggested A$ debt remained attractive to Japanese investors despite the steady fall in Australian yields and the recent upward drift in Japanese long term rates.
The typical return on a 3-yr samurai was around 5.30 percent compared to the corresponding JGB yield of 0.96 percent and virtually all the bonds carried debt ratings of AA or better.
Dealers said investor nerves had been soothed today by comments from the Japanese Economic Planning Agency that the Bank of Japan maintain its easy credit policy for the moment.
The market had thought it had sighted a possible tightening in policy on the horizon last week when the Ministry of Finance turned unusually upbeat on the economy.

The outlook for real yields was also favourable with Australian inflation expected to fall further in the December quarter and remain low for 1997. Data on manufacturing output prices today showed industry was still not able to pass on rises with the index up only 0.1 percent in September.
Annual growth in output prices was just 0.5 percent, far below the 5.0 percent levels seen in mid-1995.
"Manufacturing output inflation is simply not an issue," said Chris Caton, chief economist at Bankers Trust Australia. "This must bode well for the continuation of low CPI inflation in 1997."

The next local data of note were the Westpac consumer sentiment index for November and private sector credit for September on Wednesday. Analysts were particularly keen to see if consumer confidence had steadied after falling sharply in October. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
